scenes.text:
[CHARACTERS: Mara:F, Iris:F, Emcee:M]
[TITLE: "Gala's Silent Spotlight"]
[SYNOPSIS: "At a charity gala honoring foundation grants, Mara endures sudden public exposure when the emcee announces damaging news tied to her floral contracts. Whispers ripple through the marble hall as every gaze fixes on her, and an absent power's reach makes isolation feel like the only option left hanging."]

The room falls silent as the emcee reads the news, every eye turning toward me, waiting for my reaction.

My heel knocked once against the marble, the tap swallowed by the sudden quiet.

The chandeliers hummed above me, a steady note that filled the space between each exhale.

Say it plainly — or let it show without words?

Iris — old mentor, her silver hair catching the light as she leans in, her cheek caught the edge of a passing server's tray — touched my elbow. "The grant committee will want a statement by morning. They mentioned Dorian's name in the same breath."

My sleeve brushed the cold stem of a water glass, leaving a single wet streak on the cuff. The marble floor beneath my heels felt colder than it should, reflecting the chandeliers in fractured points of light. The heel of my shoe caught on a grout line, the scrape loud enough to turn two heads while the crowd's murmurs built like distant traffic.

Iris stayed close, her voice low. "You don't have to answer them tonight. But if you stay silent, the board will fill the gaps themselves."

The news had named my largest supplier contract, the one that kept the shop afloat, and linked it to questions about influence peddling. Every donor here knew the foundation's rules on transparency. I felt the pull of wanting someone who would cut through the performance without demanding I explain myself first.

Iris waited. The room's attention pressed like heat from the overhead lights.

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.

The emcee’s voice cracked on the final syllable of the announcement, and every head in the ballroom swung toward me like iron filings to a magnet. Iris’s fingers dug into my wrist, trying to steer me toward the side exit, but I planted my heels on the marble and refused to move.

“I acknowledge the significance of this situation,” I said, voice carrying across the sudden hush. “For the project, for the donors who believed in it, and for everyone counting on the matching funds that just disappeared.”

A ripple of whispers rose from the nearest tables. Someone’s phone camera clicked once, then again. Iris froze beside me, her breath sharp.

“You’re making it worse,” she muttered, but she didn’t pull again.

Across the cleared space, Dorian Hale turned fully at the sound of my voice. The small silver hoop in his left ear caught the chandelier light as he moved, a single bright point against the dark line of his suit. He had been speaking with the event chair; now he left the man mid-sentence and crossed the floor with the unhurried stride of someone who already knew the room would rearrange itself around him.

The foundation’s decision wasn’t his alone, he said when he reached me, but the optics required a joint statement. Under the weight of every eye on us, he agreed to the public co-hosting arrangement on the spot. The board would expect both our names on the revised press release by morning.

I felt the old ache tighten behind my ribs. My father’s abandonment at twelve had left me fluent in the language of sudden departures; I had learned early how to stand in an emptying room and still claim the space. The words left me before I could weigh them.

“My father walked out when I was twelve,” I said quietly, only for him. “I’ve spent every year since making sure nothing I built could be taken the same way.”

Dorian’s gaze held mine. He already knew. I saw it in the slight deepening of hazel, the way his mouth tightened at one corner as if the fact had been waiting for the right silence.

“I’ve spent years wondering whether anyone would ever trust me with something this fragile again,” he answered, voice low enough that only I heard the admission. “The project. The foundation’s reputation. You.”

The words landed like a hand on the back of my neck. The crowd was still watching, the emcee still holding the microphone like a live wire, yet the space between us felt smaller than the marble floor should have allowed. Iris shifted beside me, ready to intervene, but Dorian did not look away.

A server passed with a tray of untouched glasses; the crystal rang faintly as someone brushed the edge. The sound cut through the tension the way laughter sometimes does at the wrong moment, sharp and oddly intimate.

Dorian’s hand rose to the opposite wrist, thumb and forefinger twisting the cufflink once, a slow, unconscious motion that anchored whatever he was deciding not to say. He had agreed to stand beside me publicly. He had named the exact fear I had tried to keep hidden. The room waited for whatever came next, and nothing in the air suggested it would be simple.
scenes.action: I stand my ground instead of backing down.
scenes.dialogue: I'm not going to pretend this doesn't matter.

scenes.text:
A hairline crack in the floor tile caught the heel of my shoe before I could take another step toward the side exit. Iris’s grip on my wrist didn’t loosen, but her nails bit harder. The emcee’s voice still crackled from the speakers above our heads, a broken announcement about the gala’s new timeline—something about a late vendor, a delay, a cascade of dominoes I couldn’t track.

Dorian’s chestnut eyes locked onto mine, raw and unguarded in a way I hadn’t seen since the night he’d watched me argue the Stark merger with Jordan Cole. The small scar beside his left eyebrow pulled when he blinked, a thin line the color of old paper. His shoulders shifted forward just enough to cut the noise between us.

“You want the truth?” His thumb dragged once along the base of the glass, leaving a wet streak that widened toward the rim. “I want to know why you’re still here.”

The words landed. My heel rocked once against the floor tile, the sound small and sharp under the distant clink of cutlery. I could feel Iris’s breath against my neck, her silence heavier than words. “Because the board expects it,” I said, voice steady only because I’d rehearsed this moment a dozen times in my head. “Because someone has to answer for the missing funds.”

Dorian exhaled through his nose, slow and deliberate. “That’s not what I asked.” His gaze narrowed, fixing on the space between my eyebrows, the way it always did when he was about to press. “Tell me what you *actually* want from me.”

The question hung between us. My fingers, still brushing the marble, stilled. The marble was cold. The chandeliers were warm. The weight of his stare was the only temperature that mattered. I wanted to reach for him. I wanted to step back. I wanted to trust the way his voice dropped half a register when he was serious.

Instead, I lied. “I want you to do your job.”

Dorian’s mouth quirked, but there was no humor in it. “You always do that,” he said, tilting his head just enough to catch the light on his scar. “Answer the question you think I asked.” His thumb traced the rim of his glass, the motion so controlled it felt like a dare. “Try again.”

Iris’s fingers twitched against my wrist, a silent warning or a plea—I couldn’t tell which. The marble floor gleamed under our feet. Somewhere beyond the ballroom doors, the gala hummed with anticipation, with expectation, with the kind of pressure that could shatter glass.

Dorian took a step closer. Close enough that bergamot rose from his collar and the ice in his glass shifted with a faint click. Close enough that the scar at his temple caught the light when he swallowed.

“Tell me the truth,” he repeated, voice low enough that Iris wouldn’t hear. “What do you *want*?”

The question settled in my sternum. I wanted him to see me. I wanted him to choose me. I wanted to stop being afraid that his care would unravel me completely.

I swallowed. “I want to know that you’ll still be here when it matters.”

Dorian’s breath hitched, just for a second. His fingers, still curved around the glass, didn’t move. The marble floor stretched between us, slick with reflected light and unspoken words. Somewhere in the distance, a glass shattered. The noise didn’t startle me. I was already falling.

scenes.text:
Iris’s grip finally loosened as Dorian turned fully toward me, the marble floor echoing the shift of his weight like a held breath released too soon. The emcee’s fractured voice still droned overhead, but it was his eyes that cut through the noise—steady, already reading the accusation before I could soften it.

I had just laid it bare: the hidden threads I’d uncovered, the careful distance he’d maintained while the board’s expectations tightened around us both. No more evasion. The words hung between us, raw and unsparing, forcing the air thinner.

He didn’t flinch. Instead, a slow, edged smile touched his mouth, the kind that invited the next step while warning it might cost more than either of us had planned. “You always did prefer the direct cut,” he said, voice low enough that the crowd beyond us stayed oblivious. “Even when it leaves us both bleeding in the same room.”

The tray of untouched glasses caught the overhead light between us, cold crystal against the charged space. My pulse answered before I could name it, a heat rising at the base of my throat that had nothing to do with the gala’s timeline and everything to do with how close he stood—close enough that retreating would read as retreat, and staying meant admitting the pull I’d tried to bury under evidence and suspicion.

He leaned in just enough that the scent of his cologne, something unlabelled and quietly expensive, reached me. “Tell me what you actually want from me,” he murmured, the question landing like a dare wrapped in invitation. Then silence stretched, deliberate, giving me room to answer or walk away while his thumb traced the rim of a glass between us, refusing to let the moment dissolve into logistics.

I felt the fracture in the floor under my heel again, a small, private fault line mirroring the one opening in my chest. The board clock kept ticking somewhere behind the music and murmured conversations, but here, with him between me and the exit, the real pressure was whether I would name what I needed or let the distance win again.

The words left my mouth before I could swallow them back. “This can’t happen. You know that.” I felt the slip the instant it happened—my guard thinning for one unguarded second, the way it always did when the vents hummed louder than the piano—and I caught myself too late, the admission already hanging between us on the marble.

Dorian’s heel had scuffed the table leg when he moved, the sound small but final. His eyes stayed on me, steady, the kind of attention that made the tray’s untouched glasses ring once against each other. The piano drifted on through the vents, a thread of sound that didn’t belong to either of us.

He didn’t answer right away. One hand stayed at his side, fingers loose, but I saw the way his shoulders set and then deliberately eased, as though he were choosing not to close the last inch of distance. The untouched glasses on the tray beside us caught the light in clean, cold lines.

“I know what you’re protecting,” he said at last, voice low enough that it didn’t carry. “I just haven’t decided whether you’re protecting it from me or from yourself.”

The line landed with that quiet precision he used when he wanted me to hear the difference between what he said and what he meant. My weight stayed on my heels—and I stayed where I was, one heel pressing the seam in the floor tile.

He waited. The silence stretched, not empty, just held. I could feel the board’s deadline pressing at the edges of the room, the gala clock still running, but none of it moved the fact that he had cornered the moment before I was ready to meet it.

My heel pressed harder against the seam in the tile. I didn’t step back.

The words left my mouth before I could weigh what they would take from me. The arrangement would bind us in public view, every glance and gesture open to the board’s judgment and the whispers that already circled like vultures. I felt the loss of the small distance I had kept between us settle in my chest like a held breath I could no longer release.

Dorian’s heel had already stilled against the marble. He studied me across the narrow space, the low light from the overhead fixtures catching a tendon that stood out along his neck when he swallowed and the way his shoulders had settled, deliberately loose. “You say that like you’ve already counted the cost,” he said, voice low and edged with something that almost sounded like approval. “Most people lie to themselves first.”

The tray of untouched glasses sat between us on the narrow console, their surfaces reflecting fractured pieces of the room. I could feel the space between us shrink by the width of one unsteady inhale. The tray’s edge cut a cold line across my wrist where my sleeve had ridden up. My fingers twitched at my side before I caught them, the impulse to reach across the gap and steady myself against him rising faster than reason.

He took half a step forward, close enough that the scent of his cologne—something clean and unlabelled—cut through the cooler air. “If you’re choosing this, Mara, I need to know you mean it when the cameras are on and the questions start. No half-measures that leave me guessing which version of you I’m standing beside.”

Silence stretched between us, weighted by everything we had not said since the board’s demand landed. I could hear the distant murmur of the event staff beyond the doors, the faint scrape of a chair being moved, but none of it reached the space we occupied. My heel slid half an inch across the floor before I locked my ankle.

He did not look away. The restraint in his posture was its own provocation, a line he held without apology, and the console edge bit into my palm where I pressed down. I had sworn I would not let this arrangement become another place where I reached for him first. The choice I had just made made that promise impossible to keep.

The clock on the far wall ticked once, marking the hours until the next rehearsal. The arrangement would force us into the same rooms again and again, and the cost I had agreed to pay would arrive in every public moment where my need for him showed.

“I want the truth.”

Dorian’s broad shoulders filled the space between us, dark brown hair falling slightly over his forehead, the small silver hoop in his left ear catching the overhead light. He leaned in a fraction closer than the moment required, the air between us narrowing until the vent draft hit only one side of my face. The hoop in his ear tilted as he tipped his head, the metal flashing once.

“You already have part of it,” he said, voice low. “My ex-partner Alexis pushed the revocation. She still holds old leverage from when she betrayed me years ago, and she’s using your project to test whether I’ll fold again.”

The admission landed like a hinge turning. I felt the weight of it settle between my ribs. He had been watching the same fracture line I carried since I was twelve, the one that made approval feel like oxygen.

Dorian’s mouth curved, not quite a smile. “The gala on the fifteenth stands. I’ll stand beside you publicly. But only if you share one story—the real reason you need this connection so badly. No shields.”

I nodded once, the fabric of my dress brushing my fingertips in a nervous gesture I couldn’t quite control. The distant conversation faded to nothing.

Then his wrist turned, the cufflink clicking once against the table edge he had placed on the side table earlier. The edges of a memo showed beneath the flap—his own internal notes on the project’s donor list, cross-referenced with Alexis’s holdings. He had been using the entire arrangement as cover to pull her out of hiding.

The truth I had demanded now sat between us, heavier than the arrangement itself.

He waited, knuckles whitening as he pressed the folder flap flat with the side of his hand.

"Stop talking."

The board members beyond the glass partition shifted, their murmurs a low ripple that reminded us both the gala clock was still running. One of them checked a phone, the case tapping twice against the glass partition.

I kept my fingers twisting a loose strand of hair, the familiar motion steadying me even as the space between us thinned. "You want me to tell my story at the gala. Fine. But you stand there with me and affirm the partnership publicly. No hedging. No distance."

His breath quickened, the lean forward almost imperceptible before he caught it. The dark brown hair falling across his forehead brushed his lashes when he blinked. My ex used the foundation the same way once. I can't afford to look like I'm repeating the mistake."

The marble stayed cold under my heels. I didn't step back. "Then stop hiding behind her betrayal. This isn't about her. It's about whether you can choose connection without treating it like a weakness."

Dorian's mouth curved, not quite a smile, the full line of it holding the same guarded edge he'd carried since the first time we'd spoken. He didn't reach for me. A faint trace of his aftershave reached me on the next slow exhale.

A board member's thumbnail scraped the glass partition twice before he looked back at us.

I held his gaze. The story he wanted from me would lay everything bare. The one he carried still sat between us like a line neither had crossed.

My ex made certain of that once. I cannot afford to hand them another reason to question whether I can be trusted with anything that matters.”

The echo of footsteps on polished marble broke the moment I had just created, each tap drawing closer like a judgment I could not outrun. I stood my ground, my heel catching once on an uneven seam in the stone, and the words came before I could swallow them back.

"Reveal personal truth before proceeding," I said, the breath catching in my throat the way it always did when the weight of my own history pressed outward. "My father left when I was twelve. I have spent every year since measuring my worth by whether people stay, by whether I can earn the kind of connection that does not vanish the moment it is tested."

Dorian’s left foot edged forward half an inch that felt like an invitation to share a secret he already held. His heel dragged once across the marble, the scrape loud in the pause. The board’s low voices continued on the far side of the glass, but they might as well have belonged to another room.

He did not look away. “I knew,” he said quietly. “Not the details, but the shape of it. The way you reach for steadiness even when the ground is shifting under you. I saw it the first time we spoke, and I have watched it since.”

The admission landed with the weight of something he had chosen not to say until now. My tongue stuck for a half-second to the roof of my mouth. The secret I had guarded so carefully was not new to him, and that knowledge rearranged the space between us more than the proposal itself. He had seen the fracture and stayed anyway.

I forced myself to meet his eyes. “Then you understand why this co-hosting arrangement cannot be another performance. If we do this, I will not hide what I need from you in public. That is the cost. You decide whether you can stand beside it.”

His shoulders set, then deliberately eased. His shoulders rose a fraction before settling again. The footsteps had stopped somewhere behind the partition, and the silence that followed felt like the moment before a door either opened or sealed shut.

He exhaled through his nose, the sound small and precise. “I have spent years keeping my own fractures out of sight. Your willingness to name yours changes the terms. I will not pretend otherwise.”

The board members shifted again on the far side of the glass, their presence a reminder that the clock had not stopped. Dorian remained exactly where he was, close enough that the faint trace of his aftershave reached me, close enough that turning away would require a deliberate step I was not yet ready to take.

I waited for the next words, for the line he would draw or cross. The marble reflected the faint tremor in my own hands before I stilled them. Whatever came next would decide whether the arrangement bound us or simply exposed us both.
